## Introduction ##

<p class="justify-text"> 
    In this lab, components were soldered to an FPGA development board, and digital designs were implemented using SystemVerilog to verify the hardware. The project utilizes the onboard high-speed oscillator to drive a custom 2.4 Hz LED blink sequence, maps discrete logic to additional LEDs based on DIP switch inputs, and decodes a 4-bit binary input to display hexadecimal characters `0` through `F` on a common-anode 7-segment display. 
</p>

## Methods & Design ##

### Development Board Setup ###

<p class="justify-text"> 
    The development board system was constructed by soldering surface mount technology (SMT) and through-hole technology (THT) components. The development boards used for the project were the UPduino v3.1 FPGA and the Nucleo-L432KC MCU, which were connected to the board via female header pins. *Figure 1* below shows the components soldered to the board, including: DIP switches, LEDs, resistors, a capacitor, voltage regulators, and jumpers to provide power to the FPGA and MCU. 
</p>

<img src="[INSERT IMAGE PATH: e.g., images/E155_Lab1/dev_board.png]" alt="E155 Development Board" style="width:100%; border-radius: 15px;">
*Figure 1: Complete μP Dev Board with all components soldered.*

### Testing FPGA & MCU ###

<p class="justify-text"> 
    Before proceeding with the custom SystemVerilog implementation, the FPGA and MCU were individually tested using provided LED blink code to verify proper hardware function, ensuring that the soldering was successful and the flash memory could be programmed. 
</p>

### FPGA Project Overview ###

<p class="justify-text"> 
    After hardware verification, the FPGA was programmed to complete the core lab tasks. *Table 1* outlines the signal types used for the project. `led[0]` and `led[1]` were designed to map to the DIP switches according to *Table 2* and *Table 3*, utilizing XOR and AND logic respectively. `led[2]` was designated to blink asynchronously at 2.4 Hz.
</p>

<br>
*Table 1: Signal name, type, and brief description for each signal used in the project.*

| Signal Name | Signal Type | Description |
|-------------|-------------|-------------|
|    `clk`      | internal    | 48 MHz clock on FPGA generated by HSOSC  |
|    `s[3:0]`   | input       | The 4 DIP switches (SW6)                 |
|    `led[2:0]` | output      | 3 LEDs (on-board LEDs)                   |
|    `seg[6:0]` | output      | Common-anode 7-segment display segments  |

<br>
*Table 2: Expected behavior of* `led[0]`.

| `S1` | `S0` | `led[0]` |
|----|----|--------|
| 0  | 0  | OFF |
| 0  | 1  | ON  |
| 1  | 0  | ON  |
| 1  | 1  | OFF |

<br>
*Table 3: Expected behavior of* `led[1]`.

| `S3` | `S2` | `led[1]` |
|----|----|--------|
| 0  | 0  | OFF |
| 0  | 1  | OFF |
| 1  | 0  | OFF |
| 1  | 1  | ON  |

<br>
<p class="justify-text"> 
    For the 7-segment display, the four DIP switches correspond to a 4-bit binary number that produces hexadecimal characters `0` to `F`. For example, a DIP switch input of `4'b1010` outputs the character `A`.
</p>

## Technical Documentation ##

<p class="justify-text"> 
    The project was constructed using three strict hierarchical modules to meet specifications: a top-level module (`e155_lab1_ivan.sv`), a sequential counter (`e155_lab1_counter_ivan.sv`), and a combinational decoder (`seven_segment.sv`). *Figure 2* below shows the block diagram relationship of the modules. 
</p>

<img src="[INSERT IMAGE PATH: e.g., images/E155_Lab1/block_diagram.jpg]" alt="Block Diagram" style="width:100%; border-radius: 15px;">
*Figure 2: Block diagram showing the top-level routing and submodules.*

### LED Implementation & Clock Divider ###

<p class="justify-text"> 
    By inspection of the truth tables, `led[0]` is driven by the XOR of inputs `s[0]` and `s[1]`, while `led[1]` is driven by the AND of inputs `s[2]` and `s[3]`. These were implemented using continuous `assign` statements in the top module. 
</p>
<p class="justify-text"> 
    To generate a blinking frequency of 2.4 Hz for `led[2]`, a sequential counter module was designed. The 48 MHz on-board HSOSC was first divided in half using the `CLKHF_DIV(2'b01)` parameter, producing a 24 MHz clock. A blink rate of 2.4 Hz requires the LED to complete a full ON-OFF cycle 2.4 times per second, meaning the signal must toggle its state 4.8 times per second. By dividing 24,000,000 Hz by 4.8, the target toggle threshold is exactly 5,000,000 clock cycles. A zero-indexed counter was implemented to trigger a toggle and reset upon reaching a max count of `4999999`.
</p>

### 7-Segment Implementation ### 

<p class="justify-text"> 
    The 7-segment display was designed using combinational logic to map the sixteen DIP switch states to output `0` to `F`. Because the selected MAN6400 series display utilizes a common-anode architecture, the FPGA pins must be driven `LOW` (active-low) to light up their respective segments. *Figure 3* shows the schematic for how the display, LEDs, and pull-up resistors on the DIP switches were wired. *Figure 4* provides the calculations for the current-limiting resistors required to operate the display safely within the 5 mA to 20 mA range, accounting for the 3.3V logic high and the 2.1V typical forward voltage of the LEDs.
</p>

<img src="[INSERT IMAGE PATH: e.g., images/E155_Lab1/schematic.jpg]" alt="Schematic" style="width:100%; border-radius: 15px;">
*Figure 3: Schematic showing the wiring of the 7-segment display to the FPGA and DIP switches.*

<br>
<img src="[INSERT IMAGE PATH: e.g., images/E155_Lab1/resistor_calc.jpg]" alt="Resistor Calculations" style="width:100%; border-radius: 15px;">
*Figure 4: Calculations to justify the 7-segment display resistor values.*

## Results & Discussion ##

<p class="justify-text"> 
    The design successfully accomplished all prescribed tasks. To rigorously verify the logic prior to programming the hardware, `stim/assert` style testbenches were written for every module and simulated in Questa Sim. The combinational testbench verified all 16 states of the 7-segment display, the sequential testbench confirmed the counter's active-low reset and enable functions, and the top-level testbench verified the integration of the modules. *Figure 5* confirms that the outputs perfectly matched expectations.
</p>

<br>
<img src="[INSERT IMAGE PATH: e.g., images/E155_Lab1/WaveSim.png]" alt="WaveSim" style="width:100%; border-radius: 15px;">
*Figure 5: Questa Sim waveform confirming LED and active-low 7-segment logic.*

<p class="justify-text"> 
    An oscilloscope trace (*Figure 6*) was utilized to measure the physical hardware in real-time, verifying that the counter logic successfully produced a `led[2]` blink rate of 2.4 Hz.
</p>

<img src="[INSERT IMAGE PATH: e.g., images/E155_Lab1/Oscilloscope.png]" alt="Oscilloscope Trace" style="width:100%; border-radius: 15px;">

### AI Reflection ### 

<p class="justify-text"> 
    During this project, an AI assistant (Large Language Model) was utilized to help refactor an initial `$readmemb` test vector approach into the strict `stim/assert` style required by the lab specifications. 
</p>

<p class="justify-text"> 
    The AI proved to be an excellent debugging tool. When initially setting up the top-level testbench, the AI quickly identified a critical mismatch between the physical active-low logic written in the `seven_segment` module and the active-high assertions drafted in the testbench. It was also highly effective in clarifying the mathematical distinction between a blink "cycle" frequency and a "toggle" frequency, ensuring the counter limit was set to 4,999,999 rather than 9,999,999 for the 2.4 Hz target. 
</p>

<p class="justify-text"> 
    Overall, the LLM accelerated the verification phase by generating the tedious boilerplate for the 16 assertion states and catching logical inversions that would have caused unnecessary simulation failures.
</p>
